result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B is better overall. It picks one billing unit with clear reasoning, tests its revenue estimate against different average student counts, rules out per-lesson billing and fixed size bands with concrete reasons, and states its assumptions and what would change its pick. A has the better migration plan (notice period, grandfathering, contacting big studios personally), but it doesn't name the main downside of tiers (teachers bunching just under a tier boundary), and it states churn and acquisition effects as facts. B's main gap is that it never explains how or when existing teachers move to the new prices. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B covers more of the rubric. It gives a full migration plan for the existing 900 teachers (grandfathering, 60–90 days' notice, emailing the big studios personally) and names a real downside of its pick (likely churn in the middle group). A reasons more consistently and keeps small teachers at $9, but it says little about moving existing teachers over and doesn't clearly name a downside of per-student pricing. B has two weaknesses: it says per-student billing penalizes growth even though its own tiers are keyed to student count, and its definition of an active student is loose.
